title: "Can a Random Forest tell influenza-infected cells and TRIM28 genotypes apart?"
subtitle: "RNA-seq of influenza A virus-infected A549 cells, analysed with DESeq2 and a nested cross-validated Random Forest"
toc: false
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("_common.R")
n_cand <- nrow(candidates)
n_cand_genotype <- sum(candidates$dominant_effect == "genotype")
```

This project reanalyses a published RNA-seq experiment on influenza A virus (IAV) infection. Lung
epithelial cells (A549) carried either the normal host protein TRIM28 (wild type, **wt**) or a
mutant that cannot be modified by SUMO (**6KR**), and were either mock treated or infected. Two
questions were asked: which genes respond to infection and to the TRIM28 genotype, and can a
Random Forest classifier assign each of the 12 samples to its group from its expression profile
alone, without the performance estimate being inflated by information leakage?

## What was done

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  A["GEO GSE133329: 12 count tables"] --> B["Gene filter: ≥ 10 counts in ≥ 3 samples"]
  B --> C["Quality control<br>rlog, PCA, clustering"]
  B --> D["DESeq2<br>genotype × infection"]
  B --> F["Random Forest<br>nested leave-one-out CV"]
  D --> E["Enrichment<br>g:Profiler"]
  F --> G["Importance and<br>selection stability"]
  G --> H["Candidate biomarkers"]
  D -. "interpretation" .-> H
```

The experiment has a 2 × 2 design with three replicates per group: genotype (wt or 6KR) times
infection (mock or IAV A/WSN/33, 6 hours). I first did this analysis during a four-week practical
course, and afterwards I rebuilt it as a proper R pipeline of seven scripts, because I wanted to be
sure that every number is right and that also someone else can run it again. So every number on
these pages is read from the pipeline output when the site is built, and not typed in by hand.

## What came out

- **Infection dominates the transcriptome.** The first principal component, which separates
  infected from mock samples, carries `r f1(pca_var[1])` % of the variance, the genotype only
  `r f1(pca_var[2])` % ([Data & QC](data-qc.qmd)).
- **The 6KR mutation amplifies the antiviral response.** Genes with a higher infection response in
  6KR cells are enriched for defence against viruses and type I interferon signalling, in line
  with the source study ([Differential expression](differential-expression.qmd)).
- **How the genes are selected decides what the Random Forest can learn.** The planned model
  selected genes by their overall group difference, saw almost only infection genes, and
  confused the genotypes in `r 12 - m1$correct` of 12 samples. Selecting genotype and infection genes
  separately classified all 12 samples correctly, but this rule was chosen after seeing the first
  result, so the estimate is optimistic ([Random Forest](random-forest.qmd)).
- **The candidate genes mainly read out the TRIM28 state**, among them five KRAB zinc-finger genes,
  while apparent infection markers such as RPL30 most likely reflect the virus-induced host
  shutoff.

::: {.callout-note}
## Scope of the result
Twelve samples from one cell line, one virus strain and one time point: the candidates describe
this experimental system and are not diagnostic biomarkers. The full discussion of limitations is
in the [report (PDF)](assets/influenza_rf_biomarkers_report.pdf) and on the
[methods page](methods.qmd).
:::

## Who did this?

::: {.grid}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-8}
Hi, I'm Konrad. I did this project as part of a bioinformatics practical course at the Friedrich
Schiller University Jena, and somehow it didn't let me go afterwards, so I rebuilt the whole thing
until I was happy with it. The part I find the most interesting is the Random Forest, because with
only 12 samples you can fool yourself really easily, and I wanted to see what happens when you do
it properly (spoiler: the accuracy goes down first, and then you learn something about your gene
selection).

If you have questions, ideas or you found a mistake, feel free to let me know, I'm happy about
every feedback :)
